title: Same stores, less in each one
lede: RadioShack’s model was thousands of small, cheap stores close to customers. It works while each store sells enough high-margin goods. After 2005 sales per store slid, and the growth that remained came from phones, the lowest-margin thing it sold.

blocks.title: Sales per company store, 1999–2013 (derived)
blocks.subtitle: Total net sales and operating revenues divided by company-operated U.S. stores at year end, $ millions. Overstates true store sales, because it includes dealer, online, kiosk and international revenue.
blocks.source: Our calculation from the 10-K sales and store counts[^4][^6][^9][^13]. 2009–2013 use sales as restated in the 2013 10-K.

blocks.title: Wireless share of sales, and gross margin
blocks.subtitle: Percent. Wireless and “mobility” are the company’s own categories, which it redefined over time, so the lines have gaps.
blocks.source: Wireless share: 2005 and 2009 10-Ks[^9][^11]; mobility share: 2013 10-K[^13]. Gross margin 2002–2005 as reported[^8][^9]; 2011–2013 derived from gross profit and sales in the 2013 10-K.

blocks.title: The postpaid phone squeeze, 2012 and 2013
blocks.subtitle: Change from the prior year at U.S. company stores, percent.
blocks.source: 2013 10-K, “Update on Postpaid Wireless Business”[^13]. The company sold fewer phones, paid more for each one, and repaid commissions when customers stopped paying for service.

blocks.caption: The margin problem in four lines

rows.text: gross margin in 2013, derived from $1,172.2M gross profit on $3,434.3M sales[^13]
postpaid phones sold at U.S. company stores in 2013, after −20% in 2012[^13]
Target Mobile centers it ran inside Target stores at the end of 2012. It quit all of them by March 31, 2013[^13]

blocks.body: RadioShack didn’t report profit by store, so we can’t say how many stores lost money. The 2013 10-K doesn’t give a gross margin rate directly, which is why we derive it.
